message.reasoning: Alright, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's AITA (Ask if it's a thing) for ignoring my senior associate's texts. Let me start by understanding the situation. I'm a first-year associate at a local firm, and my senior associate has been there for three years. A few weeks ago, I was feeling under the weather and threw up right after waking up. I notified her that I wouldn't be coming to work because I wasn't feeling well. She was a bit disappointed but allowed me to take a sick leave. That's good because she understood that I was unwell. While I was trying to get some sleep, she kept texting me with things I needed to do. I tried to ignore it and turned off my phone's notifications to rest. After an hour, she called me and told me I had to send her a file regarding the client's data, which she didn't have on her laptop. I sent her the files and asked if she needed anything else since I was going to the doctor and wouldn't bring my laptop. She said that was all for now. I went to the doctor, who told me I was overworked because I'd been working overtime until 2-3 AM for the past two months and needed some rest. On my way home, my senior texted me again, asking for the client's billing information, something she could do herself since she has their contacts. I forwarded the information as she asked. When I got home, I took the prescribed medicine and fell asleep. I was shocked to wake up to 2 missed calls and 30 new messages from her, giving me work to do from home. I felt it was unfair for her to assign me work while I was on sick leave, so I ignored the messages and didn't reply. Now, the question is: Is it AITA for not replying to her texts? First, I need to understand what AITA means. From what I gather, it's a way to ask if a particular action is considered acceptable or not, often in workplace or social contexts. So, in this case, is it acceptable for me to ignore my senior's texts while I'm on sick leave? I think about the expectations in a workplace. Typically, when someone is on sick leave, they're supposed to rest to recover. However, in some workplaces, especially in high-pressure environments, employees might still be expected to handle some work remotely. But in this case, I was explicitly told I was unwell and needed rest. She kept texting me with tasks, which I tried to ignore to get some sleep. She called me, and I handled the urgent file. Then, after the doctor's visit, she texted again, and I responded once more. But when I got home, she sent 30 messages, which felt overwhelming, especially since I was supposed to be resting. Ignoring her texts after that point could be seen as not fulfilling my duties, but on the other hand, I was on sick leave and needed rest to recover. It's a bit of a gray area. I also consider the power dynamics. She's a senior associate, and I'm a first-year associate. There's a hierarchy, and she might expect me to be more responsive, even when unwell. But at the same time, my health and well-being are important, and I shouldn't be overworked to the point of illness. Another angle is communication. Maybe I should have set clearer boundaries from the start, letting her know that while I'm on sick leave, I'm not available for work-related tasks unless it's an absolute emergency. That way, she would understand that I'm not ignoring her but prioritizing my health. In this situation, I think it's reasonable to prioritize my health, especially since I was explicitly told by the doctor to rest. Ignoring her texts after a certain point could be justified as necessary for my recovery. However, it's also important to communicate this clearly to avoid misunderstandings in the future. So, weighing the pros and cons, I think it's not AITA to ignore her texts in this case, given the circumstances of my illness and the need for rest. However, improving communication about my availability could help prevent similar situations in the future.
